newsitem.title: GERMANY: German GDP rises, rate cut not ruled out.
newsitem.headline: German GDP rises, rate cut not ruled out.

text.p: Germany's economy grew strongly in the third quarter, according to data released Wednesday, but analysts said there was still scope for a possible interest rate cut, further bond market gains and a weaker mark.
Adjusted figures published by the Bundesbank showed that third-quarter gross domestic product rose 0.8 percent against the second quarter, when output rose by 1.5 percent.

Year-on-year growth in pan-German GDP accelerated to 1.9 percent from 1.1 percent, according to Bundesbank data, which were revised slightly down from numbers released initially by the Federal Statistics Office.
The GDP numbers came in toward the top end of market expectations, initially pushing the mark up a pfennig against the dollar before the German currency eased back.

"The rise ... might suggest that the German recovery is now very much on track," HSBC analyst Stephen King wrote in a research note. But, King added, renewed GDP weakness in the fourth quarter would end up leaving the Bundesbank's bias toward easing rates "firmly in place."

Adolf Rosenstock at the Industrial Bank of Japan, who expects fourth-quarter growth to slow to 0.3 percent, agreed: "This is just a look into the rear-view mirror, and ahead of us seems to be a rather flat fourth quarter."

A jump of 2.9 percent in October industrial orders also brightened a picture clouded on Tuesday by a sharp fall in industrial output in the same month. But analysts still expect November unemployment to rise.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said recovery was gaining strength and official forecasts -- of 1.25 percent growth this year and 2.5 percent in 1997 -- could be met.

"There are good prospects for turning the current recovery into a sustained economic upswing," he said. Rexrodt said that stronger third-quarter investment was encouraging, but only a sustained increase would cut high German unemployment.
